strengths: The paper presents a clean and genuinely useful unification: it shows that the MSE losses used by ESD, CAbl, and (in variational form) DoCo are special cases of an f-divergence objective between reverse-process conditionals, and derives practical closed-form losses (Jeffreys, squared Hellinger, Pearson χ²) plus a variational min-max formulation that covers any f-divergence.

The gradient analysis (Sec. 4.1 / App. B.1.2) is simple but insightful: Hellinger corresponds to exponentially down-weighted MSE gradients while χ² up-weights them, which explains observed training instabilities and prior-preservation differences, and is empirically validated (Fig. 2, Fig. 3).

The local exponential stability analysis of the variational formulation (Thms. 4.1-4.2, App. B.2) is technically careful, and the derived guideline (convergence governed by 1/f''(1), favoring JS and H²) provides actionable, falsifiable guidance for divergence selection.

The empirical study is broad for its scope: three anchor choices, three regularization settings, multiple iteration budgets (150-5000 steps), six concepts, single and sequential multi-concept erasure, and explicit positioning of CAbl and DoCo as special cases (Figs. 7-8, Tab. 3-7). The Hellinger method consistently shows a good erase/preservation trade-off (e.g., Tab. 1: comparable erasure to MSE with much better KID on non-target concepts).

Honest and fairly detailed treatment of trade-offs: variational methods are shown to be more aggressive but lower quality; regularization weakens erasure while improving coherence; these trade-offs are discussed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The conceptual contribution is incremental. Since all closed-form losses reduce to exp-weighted MSE on the same quantity, the practical novelty is essentially 'change the loss to exp(±MSE)', and the theoretical tools (variational f-divergence, GAN-style local stability following Nagarajan & Kolter) are largely imported. DoCo already used a non-KL divergence (variational JS), which somewhat weakens the 'first f-divergence approach' framing even though the authors acknowledge DoCo as a special case.

The empirical evidence for superiority over the MSE/CAbl baseline is modest and not always consistent: in Tables 3-7 differences in CS/CA/KID between Hellinger and MSE variants are often small and the ranking varies by concept and iteration count; the headline claims rest partly on qualitative observations (Figs. 1, 4-6). No error bars, seeds, or significance testing are reported.

External validity is limited: evaluation uses only SD v1.4, six concepts (fictional characters and artist styles), and CLIP-based metrics plus KID. Standard stress-tests in this literature are missing: adversarial/unseen prompt robustness after erasure, retrievability attacks (e.g., fine-tuning back), NSFW or personal-information concepts (the paper's stated motivation), and comparison against stronger recent baselines (Receler, SalUn, AdvUnlearn, MACE) rather than mostly MSE-style ablations of the same family.

Variational results are weak and under-analyzed: in Table 6, Hellinger (Variational) essentially fails to erase Van Gogh (CA 1.00), and χ² (Variational) leaves CA at 0.74, yet the convergence theory is stated mainly for the variational formulation. The disconnect between the theoretical analysis (local stability) and the poor practical behavior of the theoretically-analyzed variant deserves deeper investigation.

Local convergence holds only under strong idealized assumptions (existence of exact equilibrium, full-rank conditions on the critic/likelihood Jacobians, continuous-time ODE analysis), and the conclusion 'JS and H² have better convergence properties' follows from loose eigenvalue bounds in only some regimes; the practical relevance near real equilibria of neural U-Nets is not demonstrated.
Reproducibility is uncertain: no mention of code release; details like learning rate, optimizer, text-encoder/U-Net components updated, and CLIP model used for CA are not fully specified.

strengths: The unification is genuinely useful as a lens: the paper shows that the widely used MSE loss (CAbl) and the JS-based loss (DoCo) are special cases of a general f-divergence objective (Eq. 3), which organizes a fragmented literature (Figs. 7-8 are a helpful taxonomy).

The theoretical analysis is the strongest part. The gradient analysis (Sec. 4.1, B.1.2) cleanly characterizes H2 as a bounded-gradient, outlier-resistant reweighting of the MSE gradient and χ2 as the opposite, and this is empirically validated (Fig. 2) and connected to a concrete failure mode (Fig. 3, the degenerate face at step 400 with MSE).

The local convergence analysis of the variational min-max formulation (Thm. 4.1-4.2, Appendix B.2) is a non-trivial extension of GAN dynamical-systems analysis to the diffusion unlearning setting, and it yields actionable guidance linking f''(1) to convergence speed, correctly predicting that H2 and JS converge faster near equilibrium.

The experimental protocol is fairly broad in structure: single- and multi-concept erasure, three anchor strategies, regularization ablations, multiple iteration budgets (150/500/2000/5000), and a dedicated variational comparison (Tables 3-7).
The trade-off discussion between closed-form (realistic replacement) and variational (aggressive, fast semantic removal) methods is honest and practically informative (Sec. 5.3).
weaknesses: The empirical gains over the MSE baseline are modest and inconsistent, undermining the central 'superiority' claim. In Table 6, the variational variants erase Van Gogh less well than MSE (e.g., KL variational CA 0.92 vs MSE 0.71); in Table 1 (erasing Dali), H2 has worse target CS (0.62 vs 0.57) and worse KID than MSE for several preserved concepts; in Tables 3-4 the advantage over CAbl is often within noise. The abstract/introduction overstate what the tables show.

The evaluation is narrow for an unlearning paper: only SD v1.4, only six curated concepts (Snoopy, Grumpy Cat, Wall-E, R2D2, Van Gogh, Dali), CLIP-based CS/CA plus KID as metrics. There are no NSFW/safety benchmarks (e.g., I2P), no classification-based memorization tests, and critically no robustness/relearning or adversarial-prompt evaluation, even though the paper itself cites work [29] showing unlearning can be undone by fine-tuning. Given that unlearning's practical value hinges on durability, this is a significant evidential gap.

Baseline coverage is weak relative to the cited literature: the main quantitative comparisons are against MSE variants and CAbl only. More recent methods the authors themselves discuss (RECELER, FADE, AdvUnlearn, EAP, SalUn) are cited but not compared, so the reader cannot assess whether the f-divergence losses are competitive with the state of the art rather than merely with the MSE objective.

The novelty is largely a plug-in of known machinery: the variational f-divergence formulation is f-GAN (Nowozin et al.) applied to the unlearning objective, closed-form Gaussian f-divergences are standard [25, 33], and the local convergence proof closely follows Nagarajan & Kolter's GAN analysis [34]. The synthesis is competent but the individual ingredients are not new.

The convergence-speed guidance rests on strong assumptions (B.7 assumes the optimal discriminator T is attained, B.8 full-rank conditions) and on a continuous-time local analysis whose predictive validity for the actual min-max training of a large T2I model is not demonstrated experimentally. The claim that H2 'converges faster' is verified only indirectly through bounded gradient magnitude.

No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned. Given that many hyperparameters (learning rate, ωt weighting, sampler steps, regularization coefficients) affect the erasure/preservation trade-off, the absence of code weakens reproducibility, and it is unclear whether baselines received equivalent hyperparameter tuning, which matters given the mixed results.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations discussion; caveats (e.g., KID interpretation ambiguity, confined to Gaussian-output assumptions with fixed variance, applicability limited to fine-tuning-based methods) are scattered or only addressed in the appendix.

Presentation issues: the main text is dense with derivations that belong in the appendix, Figure 2 is cluttered and hard to read, and there are minor inconsistencies (e.g., mixed symbol usage for the unlearned model, non-uniform notation for x_t vs x_t^r across pages).

strengths: The paper makes a genuine unification contribution: it shows that existing MSE-based unlearning losses (ESD, CAbl, and variants) are special cases of a general f-divergence objective (Eq. 3), and shows DoCo and CAbl correspond to specific divergences/representations within the framework (Appendix A, Fig. 7-8). This reframing is useful for the community.

The theoretical analysis is non-trivial and well-developed: gradient analysis of closed-form losses (Sec. 4.1, Eq. 7) showing H² has bounded gradients while χ² amplifies them, plus a local exponential stability result for the variational min-max formulation (Thms 4.1, 4.2) using dynamical systems machinery, with a derived guideline connecting the choice of divergence to convergence speed via (f*)''(T_ω). The proofs in Appendix B are detailed and the empirical validation of gradient magnitudes (Fig. 2, Fig. 9) is a nice theory-to-practice link.

The experimental protocol is reasonably comprehensive for the scale: closed-form vs. variational objectives, three anchor-concept strategies (empty/near/superclass), multiple iteration budgets (150/500/2000/5000), regularization ablations (prior preservation, gradient surgery, importance sampling), and a sequential multi-concept scenario (Sec. 5.4).

Reproducibility is adequately addressed: hardware, batch size, sampler steps, prompt sources, and per-table settings are documented; the method itself requires only simple modifications of the existing fine-tuning losses, making it easy to adopt.
The qualitative analyses (Figs. 1, 3-5) convincingly connect bounded H² gradients to fewer artifacts and better prior preservation, supporting the theoretical story.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to Stable Diffusion v1.4 and only six concepts. Notably, the motivation emphasizes NSFW and personal-data removal, but no such benchmark (e.g., nudity/artistic-content erasure suites used by ESD or RECELER) is evaluated, and the only fine-tuning baseline compared is CAbl — stronger and more recent baselines such as ESD, AdvUnlearn, SPM, or FADE are absent from the experiments.

There is a theory-practice gap the paper does not fully reconcile. The convergence analysis predicts JS and H² have the best convergence properties, yet in Tables 6-7 the variational Hellinger method fails to erase Van Gogh (CA = 1.00, identical to the original model) and variational χ² also fails (CA = 0.74). The claim that the variational form enables 'any f-divergence' is thus weakened in practice for several divergences, and this discrepancy deserves deeper analysis rather than just the 'more aggressive' framing.

Reported quantitative margins are often small and the tables (especially Tables 3-5) are dense and hard to parse; results appear to be single runs without seeds/variance estimates, so it is unclear how robust the claimed superiority of H² is. The interpretation of KID on erased concepts is explicitly acknowledged to be flexible ('higher KID preferred' vs. 'lower KID preferred' depending on the goal), which creates room for post-hoc favorable readings.

The contribution, while useful, is conceptually modest: closed-form f-divergences between Gaussians and the variational (f-GAN-style) representation are standard, and the local convergence proof closely follows Nagarajan & Kolter's GAN analysis. Novelty rests mainly on the application and the coupling of these elements to unlearning.

The stability analysis is local and relies on the restrictive Assumption B.7 (existence of an exact equilibrium with p_ϕ* = p_Φ and optimal discriminator), which is unlikely to hold in practice; no discussion of when/why it may fail in the actual fine-tuning setup is given.

There is no explicit limitations discussion, and no assessment of robustness to unlearning-reversal attacks (e.g., relearning after fine-tuning, as in the cited 'illusion of unlearning' work [29] which is discussed but not experimentally engaged with). Given that reliability of unlearning is central to the paper's motivation, this is a notable gap.

strengths: The paper makes a clean, well-motivated unification: existing MSE-based unlearning losses are shown to be special cases (CAbl = closed-form KL, DoCo = variational JS), and the framework generalizes them to any f-divergence, giving a principled family of objectives for concept erasure.

The theoretical analysis is competent: closed-form expressions for f-divergences between Gaussians (Appendix B.1.1), a per-sample gradient analysis showing H^2 down-weights large-MSE samples while χ^2 up-weights them (Eq. 7-8, validated empirically in Fig. 3), and a local exponential stability result for the variational min-max system built on standard dynamical-systems tools (Nagarajan & Kolter, 2017), including a heuristic ranking of divergence choices by 1/f''(1).

The empirical evaluation is broad and multi-faceted: object/style ablation, sequential multi-concept erasure, nudity erasure on I2P, and adversarial robustness against Ring-A-Bell and MMA-Diffusion; results span SD 1.4/1.5/2.1/XL/SD3/FLUX, and comparisons include a wide set of SOTA baselines (Tab. 2, 4, 9, 10).

Honest treatment of trade-offs: the paper clearly delineates when closed-form losses (prior preservation, realistic replacement) are preferable to variational losses (aggressive erasure at the cost of higher KID), and analyzes the sensitivity of the variational approach to small batch sizes.

Good reproducibility: code is promised publicly, implementation details (optimizer, learning rates, batch sizes, hardware) are provided in Appendix C.1, and evaluation prompts are shared with prior work.
weaknesses: The central conceptual contribution is fairly incremental. Replacing a KL/MSE objective with an f-divergence is a well-trodden idea (f-GAN, f-SCRUB, f-divergence distillation); in the closed-form Gaussian case, all the new losses reduce to exponentially reweighted MSE (Eq. 50), so the practical novelty largely amounts to a specific per-sample weighting scheme rather than a fundamentally new method.

There is a disconnect between the theoretical and empirical threads: the local convergence analysis (Theorem 4.2) and the convergence-speed ranking apply only to the variational framework, yet the recommended default method (H-DMU closed-form) is derived without it. The theoretical result thus has limited direct bearing on the main practical contribution, and the guidance it provides is heuristic ('probably beneficial').

The variational half of the unified framework performs rather poorly in practice (high KID, degraded preservation, e.g., KL variational fails to erase Van Gogh at 0.755 CS), because divergence estimates are unreliable at typical fine-tuning batch sizes. This substantially reduces the practical value of the 'any f-divergence' claim, leaving the framework's headline benefit confined to two or three closed-form divergences.

Empirical gains over MSE are real but often modest, and the strongest headline result (nudity erasure, Tab. 4) is largely a refinement of CAbl, which is already strong; the fairness of some SOTA comparisons is uncertain (e.g., footnote 1 optimizes CAbl's hyperparameters to match f-DMU, but tuning comparability for ESD/UCE/RECE/DoCo is less clear).

The stability analysis relies on restrictive assumptions (strict convexity of f*, full row-rank conditions, optimal equilibrium) and continuous-time ODE arguments whose translation to discrete fine-tuning is only 'similar for sufficiently small learning rates', so its practical significance is limited.
The KID metric for erased concepts has ambiguous interpretation (acknowledged in Appendix C.1), which weakens the force of some quantitative comparisons on erasure quality.

strengths: The paper correctly identifies that MSE-based diffusion unlearning is a KL instance and generalizes to f-divergences, providing a unified perspective that recovers CAbl and DoCo as special cases (Appendix B.1.3, Fig. 8).

The empirical evaluation is broad: multiple models (SD 1.4/1.5/2.1/XL/SD3/FLUX), multiple scenarios (object, style, nudity), sequential multi-concept erasure, and adversarial robustness benchmarks (I2P, Ring-A-Bell, MMA-Diffusion), with many SOTA baselines compared under shared prompts.

The gradient analysis (Eq. 7, Sec. 4.1) is correct and cleanly explains the opposing behaviors of H^2- and chi^2-based losses as per-sample exponential reweightings of the MSE gradient, and the empirical gradient traces in Fig. 3 support it.
The paper is candid about the trade-off between closed-form and variational losses (Sec. 5.3) and includes an honest discussion of why variational estimates are unreliable at small batch sizes.
Theoretical hygiene is reasonable: closed-form derivations are provided (Appendix B.1.1), and the local convergence result is stated with explicit assumptions (B.6-B.8).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The closed-form losses are, by the authors' own derivation (Eq. 7), just per-sample exponentially reweighted MSE: J_H2 = -exp(-MSE), J_chi2 = exp(MSE). This is essentially the GAN/f-GAN generator loss family (Nowozin et al., 2016), whose robust-loss interpretation is well known and not acknowledged. The variational framework is a direct application of f-GAN to unlearning, and the convergence theory (Theorems 4.1/4.2) follows Nagarajan & Kolter's GAN machinery almost verbatim. The Remark claiming that per-sample weighting 'cannot be obtained with standard learning rate schedulers and gradient scaling techniques' overlooks that it is trivially implementable as a robust loss or per-sample weight, weakening the framing of this as a new capability.

The headline claim that 'Hellinger consistently dominates MSE across multiple scenarios' is contradicted by the paper's own results. On SD3 (Tab. 7) H-DMU has worse erasure (CS 0.773 vs 0.771) than MSE; in Tab. 11 H-DMU erases less (CS 0.67 vs 0.70); in Tab. 14 several MSE variants beat Hellinger on CS for erased concepts. The dominance narrative should be substantially tempered.

Gains over the closest baseline (CAbl with optimized hyperparameters, per footnote 1) are often small or mixed: e.g., Tab. 4 shows CAbl already at 0.120 I2P vs H-DMU 0.063, but RAB/MMA differences are modest, and Tab. 9 improvements are on the order of a handful of images. Given the theoretical analysis predicts qualitative differences, the empirical separation is underwhelming.

Evaluation relies primarily on CLIP Score/CLIP Accuracy and KID, which are noisy proxies for concept erasure (known to be insensitive to style-level and semantic details). No human evaluation or stronger erasure probes (e.g., membership/replication tests) are provided, which matters because several conclusions rest on CS/CA differences of ~0.01-0.05.

The local convergence analysis (Sec. 4.2) concerns only the variational formulation, which the paper itself concludes is empirically inferior and then 'restricts the scope' away from. The practically recommended method (closed-form H-DMU) is the one with no convergence theory, making the theoretical contribution largely disconnected from the main practical recommendation.

Some experimental inconsistencies are unexplained: Hellinger (Variational) in Tab. 11 shows CS 0.80 (i.e., no erasure) while the text says variational methods are 'more aggressive'; KL (Variational) in Tab. 2 erases worse than the unmodified model's CS baseline logic would suggest. These anomalies undercut confidence in the variational results.

Ethics/limitations treatment is thin: the Impact Statement is boilerplate, and there is no discussion of dual-use concerns (a method that improves nudity erasure is described, but the framework equally enables erasure of safety training or bias-mitigation features), nor of the known instability/circumvention issues of fine-tuning-based unlearning (only briefly citing George et al., 2025).

strengths: The paper unifies a broad family of existing DM unlearning methods (CAbl/ESD via KL, DoCo via variational JS) under a single f-divergence formulation (Eq. 3), and clearly situates prior work as special cases (Fig. 8, Appendix A), which is a genuinely useful organizing contribution for the field.

The closed-form Gaussian derivations for H², χ², Jeffreys, and the α-divergence family (Appendix B.1.1) are correct and yield simple, MSE-comparable-cost losses; the gradient analysis (Eqs. 7, 50-54) cleanly explains the per-sample reweighting behavior (bounded gradients for H², exponentially growing for χ²) and is empirically validated (Fig. 3, Fig. 9-10).

The empirical evaluation is extensive: multiple architectures (SD 1.4/1.5/2.1/XL/SD3/FLUX), multiple scenarios (object, style, multi-concept sequential, nudity), robustness to adversarial prompts (I2P, Ring-A-Bell, MMA-Diffusion), and comparisons to a broad set of SOTA methods (Tabs. 2, 4, 9, 10). The practical guidance distilled in the conclusions and Tab. 6 is actionable.

Implementation details, hyperparameters, prompt sources, and hardware are reported, and code is promised to be released, supporting reproducibility. The limitations of the variational variant (coarse divergence estimates at small batch sizes) are honestly discussed.

The local exponential stability analysis of the min-max variational form (Thms. 4.1-4.2) is a nontrivial, if largely derivative, addition connecting unlearning dynamics to known GAN convergence machinery.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate: the variational component is essentially f-GAN (Nowozin et al., 2016) applied at the diffusion transition level, and DoCo already used the JS divergence for DM unlearning; the closed-form H²/χ² losses reduce to per-sample exponential reweightings of the MSE. The 'first f-divergence-based DM unlearning framework' claim is weakened by the fact that the paper itself shows DoCo is a special case of the framework.

The theoretical results are largely adapted: the Jacobian/stability analysis follows Nagarajan & Kolter (2017) and Mescheder et al. (2018) almost step-for-step, and relies on strong assumptions (exact output matching at equilibrium, Assumption B.7; full-rank conditions, B.8) whose realism in practice is not verified. The convergence-speed guideline via 1/f''(1) (Sec. B.2.4) is heuristic — it bounds eigenvalues of an idealized continuous-time system at an exact equilibrium and its connection to the observed training dynamics is not validated.

Empirical support for the headline claim ('Hellinger consistently dominates MSE') is uneven: differences in Tabs. 1, 11, 12 are often small, some results are mixed (e.g., Hellinger-variational barely erases Van Gogh at 150 iterations in Tab. 11; χ² is often better or equal on CA), and the SDXL comparison (Fig. 5) is purely qualitative with no quantitative backing.

Evaluation metrics are coarse: CLIP Score/Accuracy are standard but insensitive measures of style/concept erasure, and the KID interpretation for erased concepts is admittedly ambiguous. No human evaluation or FID on a larger preserved-prompt distribution is provided.

Several presentation issues reduce polish: the change-of-variable step for the JS variational loss (Eq. 62) is asserted rather than derived; a reference dated 'ICLR 2026' appears; minor typos (e.g., 'Fux', 'Sourla'); and the abstract's 'Code available at' is truncated/empty.
